source.title: Hidden Progress in Deep Learning: SGD Learns Parities Near the Computational Limit
source.authors: B. Barak; Benjamin L. Edelman; Surbhi Goel; S. Kakade; Eran Malach; Cyril Zhang

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests grokking and gradual hidden progress on sparse-parity tasks, a different algorithmic task from the original modular-arithmetic setting.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports many parity-learning results, convergence times, architecture sweeps, and theoretical results that do not measure delayed train/test generalization or the progress mechanisms named in the claim versions; those are not included as rows. Figure 15 varies sample size and weight decay, but the text reports its weight-decay conclusions qualitatively rather than giving panel-specific numerical outcomes.
record.test_reason: In a new algorithmic task (sparse parity, not modular arithmetic), the paper reports its own result: delayed generalization after overfitting in finite-sample minibatch SGD (Fig. 4 right, Fig. 15). It also reports hidden progress measures beneath abrupt training transitions (Fig. 3, 12, 13). Grokking is a secondary, self-described preliminary result; the main topic is online parity-learning time near the SQ limit.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but the emphasis is off. The authors' main conclusion is that many architectures learn sparse parities by SGD in about n^O(k) iterations, near the SQ lower bound. They add that SGD gradually amplifies the sparse features through a Fourier gap, making progress invisible to loss and error, rather than searching at random. Grokking in the finite-sample setting, and weight decay trading generalization against optimization failure, are presented as preliminary side findings.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies sparse parity rather than modular arithmetic, and uses finite-sample minibatch SGD for grokking alongside separate online-learning and hidden-progress experiments. The finite-sample experiments use a width-100 ReLU MLP, hinge loss, batch size 32, and learning rate 0.1.
record.method_sensitivity: Finite-sample generalization and optimization vary with sample size and weight decay. The paper also reports that hidden-progress and training-curve behavior vary across architecture, activation, batch size, and training setup.

fits_no_version.finding: In online parity learning, most architectures show long error plateaus followed by sharp drops. Wide polynomial-activation MLPs show no plateau: progress is continuous and visible (Appendix C.8, Fig. 17).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Abrupt plateau-then-drop training curves without overfitting, and their dependence on activation, width and batch size, are related to but distinct from grokking.

record.problems: The grokking and weight-decay findings are mainly presented as curves and qualitative descriptions without panel-specific numerical summaries or uncertainty estimates. The authors describe the finite-sample explorations as preliminary.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant findings were omitted. The paper reports many other parity convergence-time, architecture, and scaling results, but they do not separately measure the delayed-generalization or circuit-efficiency outcomes specified by the claim versions.

untested.parts: Systematic growth of the delay as the training set shrinks is only suggested, by x-axis scales in Fig. 4 and 15. No delay times are reported.

There are no progress measures inside finite-sample grokking runs, no removal of memorizing components, and no modular-addition or Fourier circuit of the Nanda type. The hidden-progress evidence is from online plateau learning.
Entire version: no non-algorithmic data and no manipulation of initialization scale or weight norm.
Entire version: no LLM pretraining or fine-tuning.
Efficient-versus-memorizing circuit selection, a predicted critical dataset size, and ungrokking.
Entire version: no comparison of which algorithm different runs learn.
No controlled ablation of optimizer or floating-point precision. Adam is used only for Transformers, which are not in the grokking experiments.

missing.what: The m=10000 panel (no train/test gap) and the m=700 panel (fails), needed to compare delay or success across sample size for V1.
The full sample-size by weight-decay grid (m from 40000 to 700; λ of 0, 0.005, 0.01, 0.05). The caption says that with m too small the model fails, and with intermediate m grokking appears.
A control showing the hidden progress measure ρ distinguishes feature amplification from training on pure noise labels.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed to T3 because sparse parity is a new setting and grokking is a secondary result. The V2 evidence comes from online learning, which has no memorization phase, so it supports only the 'progress measures anticipate the jump' part. The V7 label rests on grokking under plain SGD with hinge loss; it is not an explicit ablation. All grokking evidence is figure-only or qualitative, and the λ used in Fig. 4 is not stated.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports grokking in finite-sample parity learning, but does not establish that the delay systematically grows as the training set shrinks.
It measures gradual weight movement and Fourier-gap progress in parity learning, but does not report removal of memorizing components or modular-addition circuits.
No non-algorithmic image, text, or molecule task, nor initialization-scale or weight-norm lazy-to-rich transition, is tested.
No realistic LLM pretraining or fine-tuning is tested.
Weight decay is varied in finite-sample parity learning, but the paper does not test efficient-circuit selection, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below such a size.
The paper does not compare whether runs converge to the same identifiable algorithm across architectures or hyperparameters.
It does not test adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point softmax limits as explanations of grokking.

rows.subject: width-100 ReLU MLP
rows.operation_detail: Minibatch SGD on a finite sample of sparse-parity data; train and validation classification-error curves are shown.
rows.measure: Training and validation classification error over training; the figure and its caption identify this as a grokking example.
rows.value: figure only; the text identifies the two center panels as exhibiting grokking, with overfitting followed by delayed generalization.
rows.note: The paper identifies the two center sample-size panels as grokking; the plotted values are not transcribed numerically in the text.
rows.check: Grokking is stated in the text, but the curve is figure only. The weight-decay value for Fig. 4 is not stated; the text says only 'with weight decay'. Training uses plain minibatch SGD with hinge loss: no adaptive optimizer and no softmax. That makes the row relevant to V7: the delay appears even though neither proposed artifact source is present.

rows.subject: sinusoidal neuron
rows.operation_detail: Tracks relevant and irrelevant weights during training as a hidden-progress measure.
rows.measure: Weight trajectories and progress during the interval when loss and error show a plateau.
rows.value: figure only; the text reports gradual movement of relevant weights before progress becomes visible in loss.
rows.note: The text says progress becomes visible in loss once relevant weights become larger than irrelevant weights; it does not report numerical weight values.
rows.check: This is the online (fresh-sample) setting: a loss plateau followed by a sharp transition, with no memorization phase. It is therefore not grokking in the V1 sense. It bears only on the part of V2 saying continuous progress measures anticipate an abrupt jump. Fig. 3 uses B=1024 and B=32, and Fig. 13 adds B=1, 4 and 128 plus a width-10 ReLU MLP, so the batch-size condition is incomplete.

source_check.locator_found: Figure 3, sinusoidal-neuron panels; Appendix C.3, Weight movement; Figure 13.

rows.subject: sinusoidal neuron
rows.operation_detail: Measures the Fourier gap in population gradients along the SGD path.
rows.measure: Fourier gap in population gradients over training.
rows.value: figure only; the text states the gap is consistently positive at initialization and amplifies during training.
rows.note: The text reports qualitative amplification along the optimization path, without numerical values.
rows.check: Measured in the online setting on (15,4)-parity with 10 trials, not in a grokking run. It bears only on the gradual-progress part of V2. Values are figure only.

rows.subject: width-100 ReLU MLP
rows.operation_detail: Varies weight decay while training with minibatch SGD on finite parity samples.
rows.value: The text states that weight decay improves generalization, expanding the range of sample sizes for which training eventually finds the correct solution; panel-specific values are figure only.
rows.note: The finding is stated qualitatively across the sweep; the paper does not give separate numerical outcomes for each sample-size and decay condition.
rows.check: The text says weight decay improves generalization and expands the range of m that succeeds. This fits a low-norm bias aiding generalization. Circuit efficiency, a critical dataset size predicted from efficiency, and ungrokking are not examined, so this is only weak, partial bearing on V5. The finding is qualitative, with panel values figure only.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix C.5; Figure 15 headings and caption.

rows.subject: width-100 ReLU MLP
rows.operation_detail: Varies weight decay while training with minibatch SGD on finite parity samples.
rows.measure: Whether optimization successfully trains to a generalizing solution as weight decay increases.
rows.baseline: lower weight decay; exact reference not stated
rows.value: The text states that the model fails to train at large weight-decay values; panel-specific values are figure only.
rows.note: The paper describes a tradeoff: weight decay can improve generalization but sufficiently large values can prevent optimization from succeeding.
rows.check: At large λ (0.05, bottom row of Fig. 15) optimization fails. The benefit of weight decay therefore holds only over a limited λ range. This is a qualification, not evidence against the mechanism.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix C.5; Figure 15 bottom row, λ=0.05, and caption.
